heading: 4 Fundamental Assumptions
evidence: • Refugees migrate in groups, and each group is a unit with ﬁxed number of individuals, whose physical, psychological and economic conditions are the same but vary from group to group.
• The migration of refugees is irreversible and there will be no ideal shield before arriving their destinations.
• Refugees are sensible who can adjust their routines as well as the weight value according to diﬀerent conditions at current node.
• The migration of refugees is progressed step by step.
• The mortality is a constant on land and another on the sea.
• Those who get their immigration granted are no longer refugees while those who enter Europe but are sent back for a lack of entrance permit are new refugees.

units.open: • Refugees migrate in groups, and each group is a unit with ﬁxed number of individuals, whose physical, psychological and economic conditions are the same but vary from group to group.
units.close: Thus it is pragmatic to make such an assumption.

units.open: • The migration of refugees is irreversible and there will be no ideal shield before arriving their destinations.
units.close: That is to say, leave out the condition that a unit go back from where it has reached to, and take no account of those who stay halfway.

units.open: • Refugees are sensible who can adjust their routines as well as the weight value according to diﬀerent conditions at current node.
units.close: Refugees are able to judge reasonably on veriﬁed routines with changing factors and decide on the probability based on the weight value of certain routine.

units.open: • The migration of refugees is progressed step by step.
units.close: Not all the refugees locate on coastlines, thus the routines head for coast are subroutines of main 6 routines.

units.open: • The mortality is a constant on land and another on the sea.

note: Four strengths (comprehensive parameter system plus AHP, PUMS-sourced numbers, seven coupled systems, extensibility to other research) and three weaknesses (subjectively chosen parameters, partly generated data so results may not replicate, no job competition so long-run unemployment is wrong). The weakness list is the sharpest in the paper: it retracts both the parameter values and the reusability of the database, and it names a mechanism the model deliberately omits. No weakness is paired with a fix, and the references start inside the last block.

note: Five strengths and four weaknesses, all as bullets, measured one line per block. The strengths are about the method (many coupled sectors, per-agent heterogeneity, robustness to scale, continuously evaluated metrics, dynamic income) and none is supported by a number. Three of the four weaknesses are sharper: dependence on current census data with compounding error over 80 years, the purely economic scope that may overstate how large an initial population is digestible, and probabilistic output that needs multiple trials. The fourth weakness (no family structure) repeats assumption eight, and none of the four is given a fix.

note: The construction chapter, and the paper's strongest modelling work. Age distribution is handled properly: survival rates from US mortality data, a 100-age quasi-Markov transition matrix, then a birthing parameter scaled to 1.08 after the unscaled chain produced decline. Two distributions are compared and the childless one is rejected on simulation evidence (a retirement bulge at year 40), which is the only place in the paper where a candidate design is refuted by its own model. The chosen split is 4000 uniformly across ages 1-20 and 6000 across 21-50, with 50:50 sex. Occupations are then derived by dimensional analysis rather than asserted: 886.869 kcal/acre/year, a 0.6 Mars growth factor, a 4.9-acre farm, 8-hour days, giving 2401.41 farmers, corrected upward to 2448.54 once parental leave is netted out. Health (10.5% of US jobs scaled by a 2.18 factor to 2287.59), research (MDRS usage), teachers (19:1), police and sanitation follow, and the arithmetic is carried to the individual worker. Every remaining sector is then assigned to government or private hands, which is the assumption the income model later depends on.

The restatement follows the standard move: define PI from the literature (a differentiation power, owned by the individual, not obtainable without permission), then announce AHP for risk, game theory for price, parameter manipulation for the extensions and graph theory for the network. The section does not state a research question; it states a pipeline, and blocks 54-56 are that pipeline plus the five-part outline. One block ([43]) is unusually long and mixes the policy motivation with the PP/IP analogy, which is why the argument there reads as compressed.

note: Six assumptions are crammed into one measured block (58) because the PDF interleaves the bullet list with the running prose, so the extraction sees one paragraph containing all six. They are: three sectors; individuals and organisations are self-interested market participants; PI sold to an organisation cannot be resold; a transaction is a bundle designed by the firm and accepted or refused by the individual; and the value of PI rises with the amount of information. Block 59 says the first four follow standard economic theory, block 60 justifies the sixth. The consequences are large and unstated: the no-resale rule removes arbitrage, and the bundle design by the firm means the individual never chooses which information to sell, only whether to sell the bundle. The second half of block 60 carries the 2.2 heading, so the notation section has no heading block of its own.

note: Three claimed strengths and five admitted weaknesses, each a bullet split across blocks by the two-column-ish bullet layout. The strengths - a concise sequential game, parameters chosen by named methods (AHP, graph theory, psychological fitting), a scale-free simulation of externality - are all method claims with no result attached, and the second is the one the body undercuts, since the AHP weights are hand-set and mu is an invented bijection. The weaknesses are unusually honest and specific for this corpus: imperfect information is ignored, no robustness or sensitivity check was run for lack of data, the parameter forms are subjective, only one-to-one trade is modelled, and the cost of self-protection is omitted (with the ownership caveat that individuals can resell). The missing sensitivity analysis is the paper's real gap and the paper names it, which makes the memo's confident pricing recommendations harder to defend than the body admits. The '5.2 Conclusion' heading is glued to the tail of block 246.

note: The pricing model is a three-part sum - expected income value, risk value, information-related value - and the chapter is really a methods tutorial for each part. Expected income: citizenship's ten indicators are weighted by AHP, with the full textbook sequence reproduced (reciprocal matrix, column normalisation, eigenvector, maximum eigenvalue, CI, RI from 500 random matrices, CR < 0.1, weights summing to 1), and the weights are then quoted to three decimals but only to two for the last entry (0.20), which is the only arithmetic slip visible. The other 16 indicators are valued by the present-value method of intangible-asset accounting, then their coefficients are produced by a Gradient Boosting Decision Tree in Python whose hyperparameters are tuned 'by adjusting the steps, iterations, maximum depth ...' with no validation split described. Risk: coefficient of variation per indicator, times an AHP weight used again as a risk coefficient, summed - the same weights serve two different roles, which the text does not address. note: The representation chapter is the paper's best construction. An individual becomes a 5-vector over demographics, family and health, property, activities and consumer data; the vector is built by an attribute-value lookup table (Algorithm 1 sums the value vectors of every matched condition), and the table's entries come from the Financial Times' price list - a general person is worth $0.0005, while 'being engaged' or 'having a heart disease' each add a specific dollar amount in one dimension. That design choice (one nonzero entry per condition) is deliberate, to keep categories uncorrelated for the later correlation matrix, which the text says explicitly. A query is a second 5-vector of requested intensity, and the raw value is v = sigma(P) C Y^T with C a correlation matrix estimated from the same feature vectors; C's off-diagonals are computed (0.82 between demographics and property, 0.16-0.69 elsewhere) and the matrix is printed in full, which is rare in this corpus and makes the step checkable. The amendment then multiplies the raw value by exp(omega T - tau t) times N^mu, with omega = 1.28e-3, tau = 9.50e-4 and mu = 1.05 taken from Information Rules - so freshness decays the value and sequence length and record count raise it, and the parameters are borrowed rather than fitted. Two problems: the correlation matrix is symmetric but the text lists only six of ten off-diagonal pairs, and the value vectors in Table 2 are single entries with no source beyond 'our database'.

note: The clustering algorithm is the paper's only original method and it is defined completely: four measurements (social circles from mutual friends plus interaction value, regions as a weighted sum of four hometown/residence distances, organizations as a 0/1 same-school-or-employer flag, and tie strength from the cited TreeIt method), each normalized, then combined into a structure similarity as a weighted inner product of per-measurement node summaries. A threshold s_k filters neighbours, the algorithm is stated as Algorithm 2, and it is run on 600 Facebook users through the Graph API, giving eight clusters (Fig.3). The distance weights alpha, beta, gamma, delta in R_ij and the thresholds s_k are all introduced as parameters 'estimated via training' and no values are reported, so the clustering cannot be reproduced from the text. The chapter closes with the network-effect function I = log(1 + sum d_i), i.e. information grows logarithmically in data volume, which is the claim the summary sheet calls 'the relationship between data and value is not linear, but log-likelihood' - the term is used loosely, since no likelihood is computed.

note: The results chapter stretches Task 1 to Task 7 across seven subsections and its quality varies by an order of magnitude. Task 1 is real work: PIDATA is 600 Facebook users, the six subgroup feature vectors are shown (Fig.6), the value components per subgroup are shown (Fig.7), and the protection price point is derived from an IBM breach study - $141 per stolen record against a few dollars of trade value, a 70-fold ratio, with a 27.7% two-year breach probability - so protection is priced as insurance. Task 2 is a survey of 77 adults producing query vectors for five domains (Table 5), and the observed pattern (health queries weight the health dimension at 0.99, social media weights the family dimension at 0.96) is plausible but the sample is small and unweighted. Task 3's supply-demand conclusion is a verbal corollary of P_agency with no simulation. Task 4 is the longest subsection and is almost entirely legal exposition - Privacy Act, GDPR (72-hour breach notification), PIPEDA, APPI's uchi/soto and honne/tatemae analysis - plus a world map of data value by country; its conclusion, that privacy should be a basic human right, contradicts the memo's position that PI is an asset to be traded, and the paper never reconciles the two. Task 5's generational argument is three paragraphs with no data, and its PI/PP/IP comparison is grammatically broken ('PI and PP are both private while PI and PP are both abstract'). Task 6 reports the mCAF conclusions (network effects exist; the community is responsible) and Task 7 reuses the lambda-and-r machinery to show the price falls after a breach, then recommends direct compensation.

note: Two sensitivity exercises, neither of which perturbs the price model. The demand one is a difference-in-differences regression of log retention on provider and time fixed effects plus provider-specific trends, which estimates heterogeneous price sensitivity - a defensible design, but its coefficients are not reported, so the section demonstrates a method rather than a result. The mCAF one is the paper's actual robustness claim: the algorithm is randomized in its initial centres, run eight times, and a metric delta compares the runs; Table 6 gives eight values between 0.013 and 0.051, and the conclusion is that delta is small so the clustering is stable. That is a legitimate stability test of a randomized algorithm and it is the only place in the paper where the same computation is repeated under controlled variation. What is missing is any sensitivity of the price to omega, tau, mu, the correlation matrix or the risk-score table - the parameters the whole model rests on.

note: Both tests are mislabelled, and the mismatch is instructive. The 'sensitivity' test runs a linear regression/ANOVA on the four country cases and concludes that every variable is indispensable, the coefficients are small, so the model does not change significantly when variables fluctuate and is insensitive to outliers. A regression of the model's own outputs on its own inputs cannot test sensitivity to anything: its coefficients are small because the specification is linear and the units are chosen, and small coefficients say nothing about robustness. The 'robustness' test then applies the same procedure to two new countries, Thailand (fixed) and Mexico (floating), gets the same qualitative policy prescription, and calls that confirmation - which is at best a consistency check on the policy-assignment rule, since the rule is what generated the prescription in the first place. The ANOVA tables in Figures 10 and 11 are never read numerically: no F statistic, no p-value, no R-squared appears in the text, so the claim that the models are 'significant enough' is unverifiable from the paper. This is the weakest chapter in an otherwise conventional paper, and it is the only chapter that claims a statistical result.

note: Five strengths and two weaknesses, all as bullet lists. The strengths are the multi-level micro-to-macro framework, the originality of proposing models 'for analyzing digital currency', applicability under many shocks, applicability to both exchange-rate regimes, and the policy-tool set. The two weaknesses are honest and they are exactly the right ones: the equations are linear and therefore fail to portray some countries' conditions, and only two countries' interaction is considered. The second is a serious limit on a paper whose entire contribution is about international currency competition, and the paper does not say how the two-country FE curve would generalise to N countries. Note the first strength is a claim about architecture and the third and fourth are claims about coverage, while only the second is a claim about content - and that one ('we creatively propose ideas and mathematical models') is the least checkable of the five.

note: Four assumptions, and the section's title promises justifications that are never written - there is no justifying sentence for any of them. The four are: digital currency is globally distributed with decentralisation, constant circulation and anonymity; every individual and country is free to choose currency without interference; digital and fiat currencies are independent, so one's value does not affect the other's; and although digital money is anonymous, states can trace every transaction at higher cost. The third assumption is the one that strains hardest, because the entire international chapter argues that trade shifts to digital currency precisely because the two currencies' exchange rates move together imperfectly - i.e. because they are not independent. Block 23 also carries the 2.2 heading and the first row of Table 1. Blocks 24-33 are the rest of Table 1, split one or two parameter rows per measured block because each table line is its own text run; the notation list is the paper's only definition of P, Y, v, e, M, prob, p_fo, p_do, d, f, λ, μ, V, pc, g, t, π, r.

note: The paper's core model and the only one that produces its own result. The setting is a one-period closed economy with representative buyers and sellers, f of buyers holding fiat, d holding digital, 1-d-f holding nothing; each buyer wants one unit of one good, each seller produces one unit at cost c; matching is random with probability min{1, i/j} so that a smaller good variety means a higher match rate. The acceptance thresholds come out as step functions of V_f - V_o against c, giving λ = 0 below the threshold, λ in (0,1) at it, and λ = 1 above - correct search-theoretic logic, and blocks 63-64 solve for the two critical acceptance levels λ̂ and μ̂ in terms of p, δ, u, c, r, pc. The three results (65-67) are the paper's most defensible output: two currencies can coexist at equal acceptance; a currency below its threshold falls into a vicious circle and is marginalised; one above it oscillates toward full acceptance. Block 67 adds an honest caveat that digital currency's low storage cost means the equilibrium coefficient may be very low. What the chapter does not do is calibrate any of p, δ, u, c, r, pc - block 122 later sets u = 1 'to make it easier to calculate', and the Table 2 parameter estimates are interpretive rather than measured, so the thresholds are symbolic until Section 4.1.2 assigns them country data. Note also that the notation on this page is badly mangled in the PDF itself (p_-o, p_-f, p_-d written as isolated subtraction fragments), which the extraction faithfully reproduces.

note: Short and structurally complete: objective (long-run revenue maximisation), cost-benefit discussion, intertemporal revenue function, tax rates on the two payment modes, regulatory cost C(u), and an intertemporal constraint. The economics is the interesting part and it is argued rather than derived: digital currency widens public recognition, which expands the tax base but shifts it from fiat to digital transactions; regulatory cost rises with digital volume (tracing is expensive, per the fourth assumption); and the government loses monetary-policy control, which is a systemic cost inside C(u). Blocks 72-74 then say the government sets different tax rates on the two modes because C(u) differs and because it needs macro-control - a two-instrument, two-target argument that is asserted with no derivation, and the first-order conditions are never written. The intertemporal constraint t + t(1+r) = t0 appears as a fragment with no explanation of what the subscripted t's are. Block 75 states the result verbally: the government 'induces' the optimal payment mix by choosing per-period tax rates until discounted net revenue is maximised. So the chapter supplies the paper's answer to Task 4 (countries modify banking/monetary models by tax discrimination) without ever showing the optimisation.

note: The classification exercise - the paper's answer to 'which countries will adopt digital currency' - is built from two anchors and a threshold. Zimbabwe is assumed to be at a foreign-currency equilibrium (it had abandoned its own currency), so its acceptance probability is set to 100% and the equilibrium condition is solved for the critical λ̂; the US is assumed at the dollar equilibrium with 100% acceptance, giving the critical μ̂. Every other country's measured λ and μ are then compared with the two thresholds: below λ̂ the legal-tender equilibrium cannot last; at or above it the country stays in fiat; at or above μ̂ the country converges to digital currency. That is a legitimate threshold-crossing design and it is clearly described. The two anchors are also the design's weakness: both are assumed rather than estimated, and the whole classification scales off them, so a different anchor country would move every threshold. Blocks 123-127 are Table 2, seven rows of parameter and estimation method, split one row per block; the table admits that several parameters are proxied by inflation rates and by 'national average of profit margin'. Block 122 also fixes u = 1 'without loss of accuracy', which the paper never justifies.

note: The simulation is described in one 335-word block and reported in two figures. Setup: two markets (a fiat market with exchange-rate conversion and policy-affected rates, and a digital market), exchange-rate fluctuations drawn from normal distributions, and repeated runs from different initial trading proportions. The 65.21% is reported to four significant figures with no confidence interval, no number of runs, no parameter table and no sensitivity, so it cannot be reproduced or assessed - and since the digital currency's exchange rate is assumed fixed at 1 by the model, the stable share is largely a property of that assumption. Section 4.3 (one 706-word block) is the paper's most concrete policy discussion: commercial banks lose the settlement agency function but keep deposit and lending; internet-finance scale effects push toward consolidation; monetary policy transmission weakens; and there are implications for less-developed economies. It is reasoned prose with no model behind it, and the paper's own strengths section calls these 'exogenous factors in section 4.3' - an accurate label.

The strengths are: acceptability is the right core variable, and the model is flexible enough to absorb added factors; the DMP-based mechanism explains government attitudes and some policies; and the theoretical preparation (Fisher plus Keynes) is 'sufficient'. The last is the least defensible, since the Fisher equation is used only in differenced form and Keynes's theory only to motivate two demand components. The weaknesses are the honest ones: the framework is large and the sub-models are loosely linked, which is exactly true (the three models share notation but no equilibrium condition); and the global decentralised market does not exist, so the model has a weak realistic foundation and the macro theory is abstract. That second admission is the paper's most accurate self-assessment and it applies specifically to the 65.21% simulation.

note: Block 54 is the symbol table (one block, 148 words) and belongs partly to 2.2 and partly here. The chapter's argument is short and its logic is worth stating exactly: total digital currency is fixed while demand grows, so the system must deflate; the authors therefore measure currency value by productivity. MV = PT with M fixed, then sigma_0 = P sigma and sigma = sigma_0 T / M, so value rises with transaction volume and falls with the money stock. Then a closed-economy identity Y = C(Y-T) + I(r) + G is added and combined to give sigma as a function of r, Y and velocity V(t), from which the paper concludes value 'will increase with the growth of the currency and decrease with the acceleration of the currency'. That inference inverts the equation - in sigma = sigma_0 T/M, more transactions raise value and higher velocity (for fixed T) does lower it, but the paper is reading a comparative static off an identity, not solving a model. The last line ('maintaining the stability of the value of the currency is conducive to maintaining the stability of the global monetary system') is the closest the chapter comes to a claim. Note the extraction splits every display equation from its sentence, so blocks 58-67 alternate equation and prose one line at a time.

note: Two returns, each defined by one equation. R1 (stability) is S(sigma,w) = (1-w)(sigma_t - sigma_{t-1})/sigma_{t-1}: the change in currency value, discounted by the degree of acceptance w - so a widely accepted currency's value change counts for less. That functional form is defensible but arbitrary; nothing derives the linear (1-w) weight. R2 (output growth) introduces capital-use efficiency theta = dV/f > 0, then K* = theta K, substitutes into a Cobb-Douglas Y = A K^alpha L^beta to get Y* = theta^alpha Y > Y, and calls the result increasing returns to scale. It is not increasing returns to scale - it is a level effect from higher capital efficiency, and the paper's own equation shows constant returns (alpha + beta = 1). That mislabelling is the clearest technical error in the model chapters, and it matters because R2 feeds the total return in 3.4 through a fixed weight. Blocks 79-84 are symbol definitions interleaved with equations, each its own measured block.

note: The shortest of the three returns and the one with the least content. Short term: if a region's rate exceeds the benchmark r*, capital flows in, supply exceeds demand, local rates fall - a correct but entirely verbal supply-demand statement, illustrated by Figure 3 which is never read beyond its caption. Long term: because total digital currency is fixed, rates rise with capital demand, and the central bank can respond by changing velocity - then equation (12) rewrites sigma = sigma_0 Y/(V(t) i) and (13)-(14) restate P = sigma_0 sigma i M and M/P = L(r,Y), concluding that M/P is inversely proportional to r and proportional to Y and that the central bank moves M to M* so that rates fall to the benchmark. The algebra is bookkeeping on the quantity equation; the interesting claim, that a fixed money stock plus a velocity instrument gives the central bank a substitute for open-market operations, is never tested and is exactly the kind of institutional question the paper's regulatory chapter should have taken up.

note: Two chapters in one heading, and the first is Mundell-Fleming in miniature. Countries are split into large (their interest rate sets the world rate) and small (rate takers), then the open-economy identity Y = C(Y-T) + I(r) + G + NX with NX = S - I(r) = CF(r) gives the loanable-funds diagram. For large countries both I and CF fall with r, so a rate rise contracts Y less than the naive model predicts and the rate settles at a 'desirable' level; for small countries NX = S - I(r) and any excess saving flows abroad. Both conclusions are optimistic and both are asserted from the diagram rather than computed - there is no elasticity, no calibration, and the diagrams in Figures 6 and 7 are never read numerically. 4.2 then brings in the impossible trinity: under the new system capital is mobile and monetary policy is not independent, therefore the exchange rate must be fixed. That inference is correct as stated, and the two cases follow - abandon the currency and accept the fixed peg plus a commodity-basket conversion rate, or keep it and float (r down, CF up, NX = CF, epsilon down). The fixed-rate case gets the sharpest line in the chapter: with reserves limited under a digital system, central-bank intervention is 'close to invalid'. That is the paper's real answer to Task 4, and it is one sentence.

note: The oversight answer to Task 5, built on a single architectural idea: everyone and every institution is a node, and the global central bank is a 'God node' with authority far above the others, with national regulators as secondary super-nodes and individuals as ordinary nodes holding read access to their own history. Block 157's individual-level claims - tax evasion easier to detect, bookkeeping gives auditable personal histories - are the concrete benefits and they cut against the privacy motivation in the introduction. The conclusion, that on-balance-sheet business disappears and banks become investment intermediaries, follows from the assumed functional form and not from data. 6.2's regional analysis reuses the NI expressions, takes partial derivatives of NI with respect to w for each level, and reports a coefficient matrix (0.0326/0.0489/0.0981/0.2520/0.2048 etc.), concluding that the national level gains most and the individual least with a small diminishing effect. Those derivatives are mechanical derivatives of the fuzzy-evaluation formula, so they inherit its invented weights; the paper reads them as economic findings. 6.3 is the most interesting prose and the least model: three schools of international relations (realism, liberalism, constructivism), then the claim that a common technical and legal framework creates a shared identity that reduces confrontation. It is a plausible argument, entirely untested, and it is the only place the paper engages with politics.

note: The chapter states its lineage honestly: the model follows Barrdear and Kumhof (2016) and Qian (2018), and the authors explain the one deviation that matters - Qian assumes central-bank digital currency fully replaces cash, whereas this paper keeps a holding ratio so that partial replacement can be studied. That deviation is the source of the paper's only policy variable (the share of households holding digital currency) and it is the right thing to have changed. The thirteen assumptions are then listed, and they are a DSGE closure set rather than digital-currency choices: no foreign deposits or trade, digital and physical money both interest-bearing at the same rate, sticky prices and wages, fixed consumption habits, indistinguishable deposits, rational households, two firm tiers with monopolistic intermediate producers, bank-financed capital, reserve rate equal to the CBDC rate, an interest-rate corridor, no retained bank funds, risk-free-plus-premium pricing, and inflation targeting. note: A complete four-sector New Keynesian model, written out with the standard apparatus and almost no explanation. Household: nominal budget constraint (1), its real version (2), utility u_t = log c_t - phi n_t - (phi_d/2)(d_t - d_{t-1})^2 where the third term is a deposit-adjustment cost, then the CBDC constraint alpha_t c_t <= d_t with alpha_t = 1 - v_t and an AR(1) for the log share of digital-currency holders, driven by the shock q_t. Firm: Dixit-Stiglitz aggregation (8) with elasticity mu, the demand curve (9) and price index (10), Cobb-Douglas production (11) with TFP A_t = exp(chi t + theta_t) and an AR(1) for theta, capital accumulation (14), bank-financed working capital L_t = W_t n_t + P_t i_t, quadratic price and capital adjustment costs (16)-(17), profit (18) and the discounted objective (19). Bank: balance sheet l_t + m_t = d_t + b'_t, profit (22) with reserve rate R^C, corridor rate R^T, loan rate R^L, deposit rate R^D, plus an AR(1) for risk-management ability w_t, the equality R^C = R (24) and the pricing rules R^D = R + r1 and R^L = R + r1 + r2 with AR(1) premia. Central bank: balance sheet (30) and a Taylor-type rule (31) with inflation coefficient phi_pi. General equilibrium: output equals consumption plus investment plus the two adjustment costs plus the two bank costs. The omission is systematic and it is stated: 'the Lagrangian equation is solved to obtain its first-order condition, which will not be explained too much here' - twice, for the household and for the firm, and once more for the bank. So none of the Euler equations, labour supply, price Phillips curve or loan-supply condition is actually displayed, which means the steady state reported in Section 3.4 cannot be checked by the reader and the model's dynamics are asserted rather than derived. Blocks 78-88 are the bank block, and they mix six equations with their symbol glosses, which is why the group spans eleven measured blocks.

Fourteen indicators are collected for countries with population over 20 million or GDP over $100bn, grouped into eight per-capita-GDP grades, and PCA reduces them to four components with cumulative variance 0.3996, 0.5505, 0.6679 and 0.8016 - so four components carry 80% of the variance, which is a defensible stopping rule. Two problems are visible in the numbers themselves. note: This is the paper's most concrete and most reproducible model, and also the one with the smallest data footprint. The data are the UK HM Treasury national risk assessment for 2015: twelve thematic areas (banks, accountancy, legal, money service businesses, trust/company providers, estate agents, high-value dealers, retail betting, casinos, cash, new payment methods, digital currencies), each scored on four dimensions - total vulnerabilities, total likelihood, structural risk and risk with mitigation. Each area becomes a point in a four-dimensional vector space, the eleven non-digital-currency areas form the training set, the vectors are projected to 2D for visualisation, and kNN with k = 3 classifies the digital-currency area. The result: digital-currency money laundering in the UK in 2015 is Low risk, the same class as casinos, high-value dealers and retail betting, and the paper's recommendation is that digital-currency supervision can borrow from those three regimes. That inference is the paper's best piece of applied reasoning, because it names the comparators and the reason (similar risk structure). Three limits are visible: the training set is eleven points, so k = 3 is a fifth of the data; the four scores come from a single jurisdiction and year, so the classifier is a restatement of the Treasury's own assessment rather than an independent test; and the chapter never reports an error rate or a held-out validation (the later 'sensitivity to sample size' discussion admits the training set should be expanded). The many consecutive `define` jobs are the definitional core of the chapter - the twelve areas, the four scores, the three factors behind each, Table 6's nomenclature and equations (34)-(36).

note: The forecasting model is the paper's most inventive move and the least justified: instead of simulating the future, it treats the world as a spatial system in which a country's banking efficiency, economic freedom and trade openness depend on its own past and on its neighbours' current values. Seven assumptions set this up - persistence, neighbour influence with global spillover, unobservables as spatial factors, capital-city distance as the metric, full trust in the Wall Street Journal/Heritage economic-freedom indices, trade as the only bilateral relation, and normal i.i.d. errors - and 163 countries with complete data are kept. The spatial weight matrix W is distance-based and row-normalised, and three equations are estimated: B = rho1 W B + B_{t-1} beta1 + e1 for banking, and the analogous models for overall freedom and trade freedom. All three are lagged-dependent-variable spatial models with a single lagged regressor, which is a very thin specification for a claim about long-run effects; the reduced form (I - rho W)^{-1} B_{t-1} beta is then what gets used for prediction. Note the identification problem the paper does not discuss: with rho and beta both estimated from two years of index data, the split between direct persistence and neighbour spillover is weakly identified, and that split is exactly what the Tunisia experiment later relies on.

note: The estimation uses 2017 and 2018 economic-freedom data and reports beta near 0.911-1.010 and rho between -0.008 and 0.089 - so persistence is strong and neighbour spillover is small, which is the opposite of what the model was built to show. The paper then works around this: it treats Tunisia (which it says adopted digital currency officially in 2015) as a 10% shock to the indices, predicts y(2), subtracts y(1), drops Tunisia's own row because the direct effect dominates, and sorts the remaining differences into Table 8. Most countries' differences are positive, and the paper reads that as an indirect spillover. The 5% sensitivity run reproduces the sign pattern. Two things make this the weakest inference in the paper. First, the shock size (10%) is chosen, not estimated, and the counterfactual assumes digital-currency adoption is the only change in Tunisia between the two years. Second, with rho of the order of 0.02, a spillover of the magnitude claimed cannot be generated by the estimated model - the differences being read are dominated by the beta persistence term, which is common to all countries - so the 'spillover' interpretation is not supported by the coefficients in Table 8. The conclusion (banking improves, GDP rises, trade openness rises) is therefore an assumption about Tunisia exported to 163 countries.

The strengths are method claims: flexible holding ratio in Model 1, four-sector coverage in Model 1, Model 2's simplicity and lower complexity than SVM, Model 3's spatial spillover idea, and Model 3's 163-country dataset. Only the last is a claim about evidence and it is the one the estimation undermines. The weaknesses are more specific than usual and three of them land: parameter values in Model 1 are partly subjective; Model 1 ignores foreign deposits and trade, which the paper admits may bias results; Model 2's computation grows with sample size; and Model 3 assumes the freedom indices are accurate. What is missing from the list is the two limitations a reader will notice first - the first-order conditions of Model 1 are never shown, so the steady state is unverifiable, and the Tunisia counterfactual's 10% shock is chosen rather than estimated.

Point 1 asks every country to build a central-bank digital-currency system, on the strength of the DSGE steady state, and adds the paper's sharpest empirical claim: at a holding ratio of 1 the economy is most stable, so issuance should proceed quickly. Point 2 lists the PCA factors leaders should improve (inflation, corruption, credit rating; broad money, GDP, budget; population, unemployment; reserves ratio, exchange rate) - a checklist that is only as good as the loadings behind it. Point 3 recommends using the KNN classifier to grade money-laundering risk by sector. (2) A country's EDPs migrate to one country as a whole, because their number is only tens of thousands and a receiving country can absorb a whole country; the block is truncated mid-sentence ('And it's better to'). (3) Accepting EDPs or donating aid is economically harmful to the receiver once jobs, living space, welfare and local discontent are counted - the assumption that makes the game non-trivial, and it is asserted without evidence. (4) Policy is influenced by pressure from other countries, which may sanction a non-contributor. (5) EDPs take the new nationality and equal rights, with negotiation for those unwilling; the UN only guarantees an option. Assumption 3 and 4 together are what justify modelling resettlement as a game, so the whole of section 5 rests on two unevidenced claims.

Pressure: P_t = [p_ij] with the pressure on j equal to the column sum, and the most-pressured country moves one step along its priority sequence (blocks 157-159). The rules that give p_ij values are: higher ranked country bears more pressure (block 161-163); stronger countries project more, capped at 8.0 (blocks 164-168); and the exact value comes from a cubic in the difference between the country's expected outcome XE and the actual X, with sign-dependent coefficients fh+ and fh- capturing political favour and hostility (blocks 169-179). The cubic is chosen so that 'bigger difference means much bigger pressure' with no scale argument, the 8.0 cap is arbitrary, and the paper concedes at block 181 that the expectation vectors and the favour/hate coefficients 'couldn't be a quantitative factor' - so the model's two most important inputs are judgement calls. note: Two numerical cases, then a stability proof. Case 1 (kb = 0.0155, kd = 0.015, p = 0.9, alpha = 0.4): the culture declines and is almost lost after 700 years, the 'complete integration' case (block 219). Case 2 (p = 0.05, alpha = 0.8): an initial decline then convergence to a stable positive level, the 'own society with limited contact' case (block 221). Note the figure panels are mislabelled - the left panel is headed (a) Situation 2 and the right (b) Situation 1 - so the readings in blocks 219 and 221 refer to captions that disagree with the panel labels; the parameter values and the described shapes are consistent with the intended order, and the extraction cannot settle it. The analytic part: eq (12) has a single interior equilibrium (M*, I*) given in block 223; the Lyapunov function is quadratic, f = a(M-M*)^2 + b(I-I*)^2 + c(M-M*)(I-I*), and its derivative along the flow is bounded as in eq (13); with a = b = 1 and c = 2 kb p /(kb p alpha - 2 kd) the quadratic form is negative semidefinite when p < kd/kb and alpha >= 2 kd/(kb p) - 1, and the discriminant condition (eq 14) gives f > 0, so the equilibrium is stable and the solution converges to a positive point (blocks 224-232). The algebra is a standard Lyapunov argument and it is the most rigorous passage in the paper. The interpretation at block 233 is the policy lever: keep p small and alpha large, i.e. limit contact with locals and strengthen transmission of the immigrant culture. That is a real trade-off, and the paper states it without softening it.

note: Three strengths and one weakness paragraph. Strengths: close to reality, because density is modelled and the 30% trigger conforms to practice, and because game theory reflects how states negotiate (blocks 278-281); practical culture protection, because measuring culture by the number of speakers makes protection quantifiable and lets policy move p and alpha (blocks 282-284); and responsibility plus ability, because the index uses emissions, density and GDP (blocks 285-289). The first strength is the one to question: the 30% trigger is a choice, not a calibration, and the paper offers no evidence that states act at 30%. The weakness is stated in one breath and is the accurate self-assessment: the game cannot predict any country's future action, and the policy cannot predict how much it shifts the marriage and inheritance probabilities, 'which make it difficult to specify our policy' (block 291). The PCA is described properly (orthogonal transformation, greatest variance on the first component, components uncorrelated) but the loadings are given without the data matrix, the standardisation, or the share of variance explained; and the coefficients are suspiciously even (0.269, 0.054, 0.257, 0.279, 0.309), which suggests a normalised first eigenvector of roughly equal weights rather than a data-driven one. The dilution mechanism is the chapter's real idea: per-capita indicators fall when refugees arrive, because the denominator becomes P + P(t) (blocks 115-119, worked on grain output), so protection capacity is a decreasing function of intake - which is exactly what makes resettlement a trade-off with the host population. That contradiction - the policy moves everyone at once, the model says culture needs arrivals forever - is never confronted.

Assumption 1 (29-34) says nationals prefer internal relocation because it is easier and because these countries are LDCs whose nationals mostly fail other countries' immigration standards - this is the assumption that carries the whole EDP count, since it makes the default outcome EIDPs rather than refugees, and it is the only one with figure support (Figure 2, block 35, 'Comparison of Some Countries'). note: Two models, both imported, both estimated on Australia. 183 gives the mechanism the policies rest on: expansionary fiscal and monetary policy lets refugees enter production as labour, raising GDP and the domestic consumer market, while a high crime rate in 'a few European countries' causes unrest - a causal story with no citation and no data. Effective labour model: Y_t = A_t K_t^a H_t^b (184, cited to [8]), with H human capital, K capital and Y output (185); the contribution share is beta times the growth rate of H (186) and CHE = beta (dH/H) (Y/dY) (187); technological progress is unobservable, so a state-space AR(1) ln A_t = c + theta ln A_(t-1) + v_t is fitted (188-189, cited to [9]). Estimation on Australian GDP, capital stock and human capital stock 1990-2012 gives ln Y = ln A + 0.573 ln K + 0.923 ln H and ln A = -0.690 + 0.738 A_(t-1) (190-191), so beta = 0.923 (192); with H growth 2.41 and output growth 3.16, CHE = 2.41 x 0.923 / 3.16 = 70.4% (193-194, arithmetic correct). Then 195 draws the conclusion: for capital-intensive countries, absorbing immigrants is 'extremely beneficial' to GDP. Two checks the paper skips: alpha + beta = 0.573 + 0.923 = 1.496, i.e. strongly increasing returns, which contradicts 185's claim that alpha and beta are output shares (they must sum to 1); and a 70.4% human-capital contribution to growth over 1990-2012 is an implausibly high residual share that would normally be read as a specification problem rather than a finding. Crime model (196-218): crime is a rational time allocation (cited to Agnew 1992), income from legal and illegal work is concave, detection probability p, penalty f_i(t_i) concave (196-197); four states - employed and undetected, employed and detected, unemployed and undetected, unemployed and detected - give incomes I1-I4 with probabilities built from p and unemployment u (198-212); the individual maximises expected utility subject to t_i + t_l <= t0 (213-214); the Kuhn-Tucker conditions (215-216) and the implicit-function derivative dt*/dw < 0 (217) give the result in 218: more social welfare spending shortens time in illegal activity, so a small welfare payment cuts the refugee crime rate. Two gaps: the derivative holds w (the welfare payment) fixed in the state probabilities, so the sign comes from one term of a four-state expression that is printed corrupted, and the model has no policing term, so the peacekeeping-force policy of 5.1 is not what the model tests - it tests cash transfers instead.

The real problem is what is not tested: the consistency check says the five weights are internally coherent, not that GNH, SSI, GDP, CPI and EPI measure what they claim, and a consistent matrix of a misconceived index is still a misconceived index. 258-260 test the effective-labour model out of sample: elasticities fitted on 1990-2012, GDP re-predicted for 2013-2016, errors 4.3%, 2.4%, 1.4% and 3.1%, 'within acceptable limits' (260, whose tail glues '8 Strengths and Weaknesses / 8.1 Strengths'). Four out-of-sample years on one country is a thin validation, and the 70.4% contribution claim still has no confidence interval.

note: Two models that are the same model with a different matrix. Crosswise (91-97): build X = (x_ij) of countries by indices (92), standardise by vector norm z_ij = x_ij / sqrt(sum_i x_ij^2) (94, cited to [12] - a 简书 blog post), write Z (95), score s_ij = z_ij x 20 (96), total S_i = sum_j s_ij (97). Vertical (98-104): build Y = (y_ij) with time instead of country (99), same standardisation (101, same [12] citation), same Z (102), same s_ij = z_ij x 20 (103), same S_i (104). So the 'TOPSIS-like algorithm' contains no ideal solution, no anti-ideal solution, no distance measure and no weights - it is a norm normalisation followed by an equal-weight sum, and the 20 multiplier merely rescales each index to a nominal maximum of 20 so the total tops out at 100. Three consequences the paper does not state: the scores are purely relative to the sample (a country's score depends on which other countries are in the matrix, so 'Australia 53.8' is not a statement about Australia); the five indices are equally weighted with no justification, although the chapter 4 text argues each measures a different dimension; and the two matrices reuse the same symbol Z and the same variables z_ij and s_ij across equations (13) and (14) for a completely different meaning, so the notation cannot distinguish a country score from a year score.

note: One 58-word paragraph is the entire sensitivity analysis: each of the five indicators was changed by 5% and 10%, a new score was computed, and the result is 'a linear relationship between the scores and figures of indicators', with the total score also responding linearly. Two things follow. First, the finding is a tautology: the model is s_ij = 20 x_ij / sqrt(sum x^2), so a common scaling of an indicator changes the score by a known algebraic factor with no interaction between indices - there is nothing else a perturbation could show. Second, and more seriously, the perturbation that matters is not tested: whether the India-Japan gap of 0.25 points (108) survives a change in the sample of countries, since the norm normalisation makes every score depend on the other four countries in the matrix. Changing one indicator by 5-10% within a fixed five-country matrix cannot answer that. The chapter has no table, no numbers and no figure, and it is followed immediately by the strengths chapter, so the paper's robustness claim rests on a single sentence.

heading: 4.1.3 Diagnosis of Health Conditions (OPG eq. 3, health classes, Figure 9)
evidence: We use a simple acceptance/rejection model (0-1 model) to determine the health conditions.
The overall health condition can be measured with point gain and the occuring problem can be located.
We caculate the point gain with the equation below: 14 ∑ OPG = ωipi (3) i=1 …
Overall point gain (OPG) describes the health condition of a system, but only when its value is 1 can it prove that the system is completely healthy.
We have classiﬁed the health status as follows: …
• Healthy: OPG = 1, showing that all indicators are normal.
• Sub-healthy: OPG ⩾0.9, showing that the system has small problems.

heading: 8 Model Evaluation and Further Discussion (8.1 Strengths, 8.2 Weaknesses, 8.3 Further Discussion)
evidence: 1. The selection of evaluation indicators is scientific and comprehensive.

heading: 2.3 Assumptions (ten numbered assumptions)
evidence: 1. No matter how well basic education is done, it cannot replace the role of higher education, and the same principle applies.
2. Quantity is the prerequisite for quality.
3. All sectors of society (whether public or private) can measure their investment in higher education with currency.
4. Unfairness in higher education mainly comes from economic factors and social status.
5. The labor market in a market-economy-country is a buyer's market, and the jobs are mainly provided by the pillar industries of the national economy and their derivative industries.
6. The policies in our models do not include the promises of politicians participating in elections to voters in elections.
7. Without the influence of strong policies, the changes in various indicators of the health of higher education are very slow.
8. Higher education institutions set up by the government is more focused on justice, while private institutions to focus more on efficiency.
9. The same indexes with different statistical calibers had similar trends over time.
10. External shocks such as the COVID-19 and the financial tsunami are not taken into account.

That last number is the honest one: one of the three dimensions is projected to be unchanged by the policies, and it is reported as a result rather than as a failure. 229 concludes that by 2040 S = (0.58, 0.61, 0.50) with a deviation angle under 11.5 degrees, 'which shows our policies are really effective'. Recomputing that vector gives modulus sqrt(0.58^2 + 0.61^2 + 0.50^2) = 0.979 and a deviation angle of about 4.9 degrees against S0, matching the summary sheet's '0.978 and 4.86 degrees'. note: The state-funded case, judged indicator by indicator. 123-124 is one visual paragraph (the rendered page shows the premise sentence and the division-of-labour sentence in the same block of text, split by the measure after 'between countries.'), so it is one group: mining as inter-state economic activity, with labour from less-developed countries, finance and technology from developed ones, rough processing where labour is cheap, final processing and sales in developed countries, profits shared, and tax revenue improving welfare. Then each bullet is one group, the bullet symbol left stranded at a line end and the reasoning spread over 4-7 measured lines: Civ1 125-131 (new market, jobs, industry transformation, but incremental on an existing mining base so both country types get 'moderate impact' with scope for 'significant'), Civ2 132-137 (developed countries gain significantly because they can do the science; less-developed mostly moderate), Eco1 138-142 (capital per capita tracks income per capita - and the sentence is printed twice inside the group, 138-139 and again 140-142, a copy-paste duplication), Eco2 143-149 (word-for-word identical to the Civ1 judgement), Eco3 150-154 (poverty falls a little, moderate in small countries), Eco4 155-159 (traditional industries touched, not transformed), Env1 160-163 (moderate), Env2 164-167 (moderate because of transport costs and deployment lag), Soc4 168-174 (urbanisation rises but private-led development limits it - a reference to the *other* case inside the state-funded section), and 175-178 dismisses Gov1, Gov2, Soc1, Soc2, Soc3 and Soc5 as unaffected. Note that Civ1 and Eco2 are the same variable twice (income per capita appears as both a civilization and an economy index) and they receive the same judgement twice, so one of the fifteen factors is effectively counted twice. 179 defines the two single-factor matrices R1 and R2 (printed as (11) and (12); the OCR shows only row fragments), 180 is the fuzzy product B_i = A*R_i with B1 = (0.234, 0.462, 0.233, 0.050, 0.021) summing to 1.000 and B2 = (0.237, 0.571, 0.192, 0.050, 0.021) summing to 1.071, which is not a membership vector. 181 scores them: IM1 = 2.332 and IM2 = 2.312. Recomputing with the stated scores {5,2,1,-2,-5} gives 5(0.234)+2(0.462)+0.233-2(0.050)-5(0.021) = 2.122 for the developed group, so the printed IM1 is 0.21 too high, while IM2 (2.314), IM3 (2.006) and IM4 (1.709) all reproduce to within 0.003. That single misprint is what the next chapter's conclusions turn on.

note: The chapter where the two cases are compared, and where the arithmetic breaks. 229 is the 4.3 heading. 230-231 is conclusion 1: IM1 > IM3 and IM2 > IM4, i.e. state funding benefits both country types more than private funding (2.332 > 2.003 and 2.312 > 1.708; both hold on the printed values). 232-234 is conclusion 2: with Delta_IM12 = IM1 - IM2 and Delta_IM34 = IM3 - IM4, the claim is Delta_IM12 > Delta_IM34, i.e. the developed/less-developed gap is smaller under state funding. On the printed numbers 2.332 - 2.312 = 0.020 against 2.003 - 1.708 = 0.295, so the inequality is false and the conclusion is the opposite of what the values say. If IM1 is corrected to the recomputed 2.122, then Delta_IM12 = -0.190, whose magnitude 0.190 does satisfy |Delta_IM12| < |Delta_IM34| = 0.295, so the intended comparison needs absolute values and a corrected IM1 - the chapter's central claim survives only after both a numerical repair and a sign convention that the text never states. Note also how small the state-funding gap is (0.02 on a scale from -5 to 5) even before that repair: the 'equity-promoting' difference is essentially zero. 235 converts conclusions 1 and 2 into 'state-sponsored asteroid mining can promote global equity, which is consistent with what we know to be true' - an appeal to prior belief in place of the failed test. 236-238 explain why: state projects resemble a planned economy with macro-control, contractual output and prices, and can carry science benefits to poor partners, while multinational mining is an oligopoly or monopoly in which weak countries share neither technology nor results. The reasoning is sound; it is the measurement that does not carry it.

heading: 5 Policies Could Be Implemented (5.1 Economic Aspects, 5.2 Civilization Aspects, 5.3 Industry Aspects)
evidence: Considering that in task 1, economy and civilization have greater impact on global equity, and that the development of science and technology is the main part of the civi- lization, we pay more attention to promoting equity in these two areas when formulat- in …
Asteroids should not become new colonies for a few countries, and any attempt to colonize them should be severely condemned and stopped.

We encourage cooperation between technologically advanced countries and less advanced countries, and stipulates that a certain proportion of mining conducted by technologically advanced countries should be cooperated with developing countries.
In international cooperation, the country providing labor should be counted as a partner, instead of just an employee, that is to say, it should participate in the dis- tribution of the end beneﬁts.
Countries are allowed to license certain mining projects to private companies, but the amount of license should be limited.
In order to facilitate the efﬁciency of international trade markets, countries involved should reduce tariffs on asteroid mining related industries.

Asteroid mining should be based on the premise of peace, and all economic losses caused by violent acts should be borne by the country that starts the violence, and compensation should be made for the losses.
Some of the resources from asteroid mining should be used for scientiﬁc research.
In cooperation, technologically advanced countries are obliged to provide certain technical support to poor countries, and technological communications between coun- tries are encouraged.
Any actions that limit the free mobility of visiting scholars or students among coun- tries for reasons of protecting core skills is not supported.
In principle, there should be some concessions for the use of new intellectual prop- erty generated by the development of the asteroid mining industry.
In all mining and subsequent production processes, the accident rate needs to be controlled.
Space debris generated during asteroid mining should be properly disposed of.
Mineral industry chain mainly consists of four parts: basic geology and theoretical work research; prospecting; mining; raw ore processing.
The previous policy requires the government to guarantee a certain amount of in- ternational cooperation.
If the government chose not to do so, the mining project would either funded by the government or by private companies that have bought the mining right from the government.
The speciﬁc mining process is divided into two parts: transportation and space mining.
Raw ore processing is entrusted by countries with abundant technology or capital to countries or regions with abundant energy and labor.

note: 20 blocks, 6 groups: a lead-in and five assumption/justification pairs, each pair split over 2-5 measured blocks because the justification wraps line by line. (1) mining is 'technically feasible, and financially worth the investment' — 'This is the basis for the whole model.'; (2) 'Only a few countries ... will have the relevant technology' — justified as a route into Cournot-Nash equilibrium; (3) actors are rational and maximise utility — justified only by tractability ('the complexity of calculation will be greatly increased'); (4) mining will be done by private companies with possible state investment, justified on the US Commercial Space Launch Competition Act; (5) 'Our data sources are reliable and accurate' — justified circularly ('Since our data comes from international data sites, we assume that the data is reliable'). Every job is limit, not derive, because no assumption is tested or quantified; assumption 5 is the one the sensitivity analysis later tries to buy back with gaussian noise. heading: 3 Establish the D&E Model (definition and requirements)
evidence: 3 Establish the D&E Model Global equity means that countries have access to the resources and opportuni- ties that bring about similar levels of development.
• Universal: The model should be universal and can be used to compare the de- velopment equity of different countries in the world, so the indicators we choose should be applicable to most countries.

heading: 4.1 Who can Do the Mining
evidence: 4.1 Who can Do the Mining We believe that mining asteroids will be feasible at some point in the future, and that the beneﬁts of this act will cover its costs, which means the act will be proﬁtable.

heading: 6 Policy Proposal (6.1 Mandatory, 6.2 Incentive)
evidence: 6 Policy Proposal While the Outer Space Treaty gives principles to be followed, it lacks speciﬁcity in implementation.

• In order to facilitate management and maximize the use of resources, we estab- lished the Asteroid Mining Organization (AMO) , an agency of the United Na- tions Ofﬁce for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA), to manage all aspects of asteroid mining.
• States must apply to AMO for certiﬁcation of technology level, which is passed in order to obtain a license for outer space mining.
• States that mine in space must declare their true income and pay taxes in the form of raw materials or currency.
• States should protect the environment in outer space during mining, and those that damage the environment will be required to restore it and ﬁned.
• States shall not place nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit or on celestial bodies, nor shall they wage war.
• We encourage countries to extract minerals for sustainable development rather than temporary economic proﬁt, which means controlling the total amount and rate of extraction.
• We encourage developed countries to provide economic assistance to develop- ing countries, including but not limited to providing funds, jobs.
• We encourage countries to share advanced technologies for the development of the planet, rather than building technological barriers through patents.
• We encourage countries to increase the diversity of minerals and conduct re- search accordingly, which may provide an unanticipated boost to the develop- ment of science and technology.
• We encourage countries to establish environmental protection foundations for research on green technologies and environmental remediation.

heading: 9 Model Evaluation and Further Discussion (9.1 Strengths, 9.2 Weaknesses)
evidence: 9 Model Evaluation and Further Discussion 9.1 Strengths …

• Our model uses data from 35 countries spanning 10 years as a sample for pre- diction, the data coverage is wide, the time span is long, and the pre-processing is scientiﬁc, making our ﬁndings more credible.
• We considered economic, technological, and ecological indicators in our mod- eling to measure the degree of development in a more comprehensive way.
• We have combined the advantages of Entropy Weight Method and Coefﬁcient of Variation Method to achieve diversity while ensuring the objectivity of the model.

• We creatively used the distance from each sample point to the center point to measure the degree of equity, creating the Dimensional Adaptive Equity As- sessment Model, which quantiﬁes a relatively subjective concept.

• We divide the process of asteroid mining into two parts, production and distribu- tion, and build the Production and Allocation Model, which ensures feasibility while simplifying and allows us to study the impact of changing conditions more clearly.
• Our equity index is a composite score, which means that we can only get an overall picture of equity, not the speciﬁc structure.
• When we analyze the impact of asteroid mining on the equity of countries, we act the changes on the superior indicators rather than the more basic inferior indicators.
• For simpliﬁcation, we used second-order difference equations to ﬁt the develop- ment process, which may deviate from reality.

Assumption 1 says asteroid resources are unlimited, which is assumed only “to make our discussion of long-round trend possible”; assumption 2 immediately says that at any moment the usable stock is “limited and scarce”, and defends that as the source of inequity. note: 60 measured blocks, 819 words, 34 printed units — a taxonomy, not prose: every indicator gets a numbered label and a one- or two-line gloss, and the line breaker split the glosses, so the group boundaries follow the labels rather than the blocks. Natural resources (58-73) has four indexes: PDI, the rank correlation between production and demand, where “the closer the correlation coefficient is to 1, the fairer the allocation”; IOI, the coefficient of variation of imports and exports; and two concentration indexes, HHIRO for occupancy and HHIRC for consumption, both of them Hirschman-Herfindahl sums of squared country shares. The HHI formula in 66 is printed correctly (sum of S_i^2) but the text before it calls HHI “a comprehensive index to measure industrial concentration” and then applies it to resource occupancy, which is an analogy, not a derivation. Economy (74-80) uses Gini of wealth per capita and Theil of GDP per capita; life quality (81-94) uses Moran's I, the only place where a real derivation appears (81-85), applied to PPI, poverty share and urban population ratio; environment (95-105) uses four Moran indexes (carbon, effluent, solid waste, pollution-control investment); health and education (106-117) uses coefficients of variation of compulsory-education completion, infant mortality and access to health resources, the last built as the average of three sub-indicators. Two structural observations: every index is a *dispersion* measure (rank correlation, CV, HHI, Moran, Gini, Theil), so a high HELEN score means countries are similar, not that they are well off — the same property as the GE definition in the other 2022 papers, and it is never stated; and six of the fourteen indicators are Moran indexes whose weights depend on a contiguity matrix that is never printed or tested for sensitivity.

The model itself is simple and worth recording exactly. Three indicators: global temperature B1, environmental pollution B2, ecosystem balance B3, each given a paragraph of motivation rather than a measurement (74-86). Four rubric levels: Green, Sub-Green, Normal, Bad (89-93), defined against the 2020 distribution of the 46 countries rather than against any absolute standard — Normal is literally “average of current climate protection in 2020”. Equations (3)-(6) build a data matrix D (3×46), a quantile matrix Q of minimum and three quartiles, a piecewise-linear membership function for each level, and the aggregate β = Weight·A. The AHP weight vectors are printed as (7): WB1 = (0.7402, 0.0757, 0.1840), WB2 = (0.0955, 0.6542, 0.2502), WB3 = (0.1428, 0.1428, 0.7142) — the third row is suspiciously exactly a repeat of 1/7, 1/7, 5/7, and no comparison matrix, eigenvalue or consistency ratio is printed anywhere for these three vectors, which makes them unverifiable in a way the 2023-2305794 AHP weights are not. 104-106 aggregate the 46 country vectors by GDP share into a world vector and define Score = 2w1 + 1w2 − 1w4 with range [−1, 2], silently dropping w3; the score scale therefore depends on w3 being small, which is never checked. 108-110 report that scores move toward (2, 2, 2) with GGDP.

The two cost bullets are the equity ones: intergenerational equity (142-152), where the paper reports the ethical dispute between deep immediate cuts and incremental action and then says GGDP forces countries to use fewer resources, which is “difficult for some policy makers who are shortsighted”; and regional equity (153-160), where the externality requires cooperation and the weight given to underdeveloped regions, plus transfer mechanisms. The three benefit bullets (6.1.2) are mechanism arguments rather than measurements: sustainable development because the accounting forces polluting industries down (161-166); economic growth because GGDP still contains GDP as its body (167-171); and moderate change because only “a small portion of their industries” needs adjusting, which “would prevent the economy from experiencing drastic fluctuations” (172-176). The costs are argued in the language of political feasibility and the benefits in the language of accounting identity, and nothing in this chapter is quantified; it is the qualitative frame that section 6.3 then tries to quantify with OLS.

However, these regulations only make a principled provision, which cannot decline illegal wildlife trade(IWT) effectively, and there are still many people hunting, smuggling, and selling endangered wildlife for proﬁt.

In an effort to provide more personalized analysis and service and to effectively re- duce the incidence of illegal wildlife trading, the government of the United Republic of Tanzania was selected as our client.
In terms of power, the Tanzania Government has a presidential system of govern- ment.
In terms of resources, Tanzania’s ﬁscal revenues are able to support the economic growth-based programs we offer.
In terms of interest, Tanzania has always been committed to the protection of wildlife and has acted on it for a long time.
We believe that our programs to reduce the illegal trade in wildlife are in line with the interests of the Tanzanian government.
Therefore, the Tanzanian government has full capacity and interest to adopt our project and carry out this noble work of reducing illegal hunting of wildlife.
For convenience, we draw a frame chart (Figure 1) to represent our work.

The model has no carrying capacity and no saturation, so poached-animal growth is exponential in W with the per-capita rate r1 + µ − τ1M; the paper calls this 'the modified Lotka-Volterra equation' but a classic predator-prey system would put the prey's self-limitation in a −W²/K term, and none is present. And the sign of the enforcement term is backwards relative to the strategy narrative: τ1 appears with a minus sign on W, which the text at 165 reads as 'the ability of the amount of ... resources invested to stop poaching incidents', while τ2 multiplies enforcement's response to W — so enforcement enters both equations and the paper never checks the equilibrium or stability of the pair, though it later interprets simulation paths from it (248, 263). 173-177 are one paragraph of parameter-sign commentary split over five blocks; 178-180 are strategy II (law enforcement, development assistance, whistle-blowing).

heading: 1 Introduction (1.1 Problem Background, 1.2 Restatement of the Problem, 1.3 Global Cybersecurity Index)
evidence: 1. Introduction 1.1 Problem Background Cybercrime, which refers to the use of a computer as an instrument to further illegal ends, has been evolving alongside technological advancements and has become an inevitable threat especially in this digital age.
Therefore, many countries have implemented relevant policies to prevent cybercrime.

In this problem, we are going to help identify patterns that could inform the data- driven development and refinement of national cybersecurity policies and laws based on those that have demonstrated effectiveness.

Identify parts of a policy or law that are particularly effective or ineffective in addressing cybercrime by exploring the published national security policies of various countries and comparing these with the distribution of cybercrimes.

Finally, based on the quantity, quality, and reliability of the data, limitations or concerns that national policy makers should consider when relying on our work to develop or refine their national cybersecurity policies will be explained.

Fig.2 Our work As shown in Figure 2, our work can be divided into four stages Stage I Data Preparation Based on the specific rules of the VERIS framework, we purposefully filtered certain variables and built a robust data preprocessing system.

Stage II High Risk Region Location Using the cybercrime records in the VCDB and other indicators reflecting regional cybercrime risk levels, we developed a plausible risk assessment model and created a visualization system to represent global risk levels.
Based on the collected cybercrime records, we identified apparent crime trends in specific countries.
Using data provided by the World Bank, we selected a subset of indicators that are theoretically relevant to cybercrime activities.

evidence: In this study, we tackled the growing challenge of cybercrime by developing models to evaluate the effectiveness of cybersecurity policies and predict cybercrime trends based on country-specific characteristics.

note: 4 blocks, about 278 words. 170-171 are the two strengths: DID controls time-invariant unobservables and reduces selection bias, and SEM handles multiple dependencies with latent variables. Both are textbook properties of the methods rather than properties of this application, and neither mentions any result. 171's tail carries '9.2 Weaknessess' (sic). 172-173 are the two weaknesses: unobserved time-varying confounders and the panel-data burden for DID, plus SEM's linearity, sample-size and outlier sensitivity.
